claims.arxiv2609_06718: One deployable humanoid control policy, driven by high-level skill commands, can carry out several different ball-interaction skills, switch between them on command, and complete long sequences of them after being transferred from simulation to a real robot. Supported only if, under an equal training budget, its full-sequence success rate is strictly higher than that of the strongest earlier single-stage multi-skill controller at both evaluated sequence lengths, and its success rate on the physical robot is strictly higher than a matched conventional motion-prior controller on every atomic and composite task evaluated. Full-sequence success means completing every commanded subskill in order, not merely reaching some intermediate stage.

0.text: Confirm the policy can do the individual skills before testing sequences. Setup: train five approaches, including plain reinforcement learning, an adversarial motion-prior method and two conditional variants, in the same simulator on the same 25-DoF humanoid with identical settings, observation space, task rewards, reference motions, evaluation protocol and shared hyperparameters. Evaluate 100 trials per atomic task with randomisation and observation corruption switched off. Trapping starts a ball 1-2 m away at 0.5-1.5 m/s and succeeds if its speed drops below 0.3 m/s within 20 s; dribbling starts it 0.5-1 m away and succeeds on reaching a sampled target within 20 s; shooting starts the robot 4-6 m out and succeeds if the ball crosses the goal line within 15 s. Result: the proposed policy reaches 95% shooting, 100% trapping and 100% dribbling. The adversarial baseline is close behind at 87/99/94, while the two conditional variants collapse on shooting and dribbling (1% and 1%, 8% and 36%) and plain reinforcement learning fails at 9%/97%/5%.

1.text: Full command-driven sequences under a shared budget. Setup: six approaches, same rewards, same maximum training budget, randomised initial conditions, 1,000 sequential single-environment trials each, with commands switching on events. The medium sequence is dribble then shoot, succeeding only if the ball enters the goal within 30 s; the hard sequence is trap, three dribbles through waypoints, then shoot, within 40 s. Substage rates are conditional on reaching that stage, while overall success requires every stage in order. Result: on the medium sequence, 88.0% overall for the proposed policy against 67.2% for the strongest baseline, with 51.0% and 42.6% for two others and 0.0% for plain reinforcement learning. On the hard sequence, 81.7% against 45.6% for the strongest baseline, 27.4% and 5.0% for the others, and 0.0% for plain reinforcement learning. The margins are 20.8 and 36.1 points.

4.text: Does trapping survive a stricter definition of success? Setup: redefine first contact as the ball coming within 0.4 m and require that, within 3 s after contact, the ball stays below 0.25 m/s and within 0.5 m of the robot for at least half a second, over 100 trials per method. Result: 63% for the proposed policy against 31%, 24% and 50% for the three baselines. All methods fall sharply from the near-100% trapping numbers measured under the looser rule, so the headline trapping figures are sensitive to how success is defined.

5.text: Does it work on the physical robot? Setup: run the proposed policy and the standard adversarial motion-prior baseline for 10 hardware trials each on four motion-capture-based tasks: dribbling to a target region, shooting at the goal, two-step dribbling with a direction change, and dribble-then-shoot. Composite commands are triggered by hand when the current subtask finishes. A trial succeeds only if the robot completes the objective without falling and the ball stays in bounds, with composite success requiring every subtask in order. Result: the baseline succeeds in 1, 1, 0 and 0 of 10 trials; the proposed policy in 8, 8, 7 and 6, so it is strictly higher on all four tasks.

notes: Nearly the whole paper was visible at 18 pages. [4] now states that all methods fall sharply under the stricter trapping rule, so the headline numbers depend on the success definition; v3 gave the numbers without that reading.
